subject: Mathematics
name: Mathematics, Year 8
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Rational and irrational numbers
points.brief: A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers. An irrational number, such as π or √2, cannot, and its decimal never ends or repeats.

points.title: Multiplying and dividing powers
points.brief: With the same base, multiply powers by adding the indices and divide by subtracting them, so 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁶ and 5⁷ ÷ 5³ = 5⁴.

points.title: Power of a power and the zero index
points.brief: A power raised to a power multiplies the indices, so (2³)² = 2⁶, and any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1.

points.title: Terminating and recurring decimals
points.brief: Dividing top by bottom turns a fraction into a decimal that either ends, such as 3/8 = 0.375, or repeats, such as 1/3 = 0.333..., shown with a dot or bar.

points.title: Multiplying and dividing integers
points.brief: Two numbers with the same sign multiply or divide to a positive, and different signs give a negative, so −6 × −3 = 18 and 20 ÷ −4 = −5.

points.title: Operations with negative fractions and decimals
points.brief: The sign rules for integers also apply to negative fractions and decimals, such as −1/2 × 3/4 = −3/8.

points.title: Percentage increase and decrease
points.brief: Find a new amount after a percentage change by multiplying by a single factor, such as 1.15 for a 15% increase or 0.8 for a 20% decrease.

points.title: Profit, loss and percentage change
points.brief: Profit or loss is selling price minus cost price, and percentage change is the change divided by the original amount, times 100.

points.title: Collecting like terms
points.brief: Like terms have the same variables with the same powers, such as 3x and −5x, and only like terms can be added or subtracted.

points.title: Expanding brackets
points.brief: The distributive law multiplies each term inside the brackets by the term outside, so 3(2x − 4) = 6x − 12.

points.title: Factorising by the highest common factor
points.brief: Factorising is the reverse of expanding, taking out the highest common factor, so 8x + 12 = 4(2x + 3).

points.title: Properties of operations in algebra
points.brief: The commutative, associative, identity and inverse properties explain why terms can be reordered and regrouped when simplifying, such as a + b = b + a.

points.title: Equations with brackets and variables on both sides
points.brief: Expand any brackets, collect the variable terms on one side and the numbers on the other, then solve, so 5x − 3 = 2x + 9 gives x = 4.

points.title: Solving one-variable inequalities
points.brief: Inequalities are solved like equations, and the solution, such as x > 3, is a range of values shown on a number line with an open or closed circle.

points.title: Graphing linear relations
points.brief: A rule such as y = 2x − 1 gives a table of values whose points lie on a straight line when plotted.

points.title: Solving an equation from a graph
points.brief: The x-value where a line reaches a given y-value solves the matching equation, and two lines cross where both rules are true.

points.title: Linear models
points.brief: A fixed amount plus a rate, such as a $20 fee plus $15 an hour, gives a linear rule, C = 15h + 20, where the rate sets the steepness.

points.title: Area of trapeziums, rhombuses and kites
points.brief: A trapezium's area is half the sum of the parallel sides times the height, and a rhombus or kite's is half the product of its diagonals.

points.title: Area and perimeter of composite shapes
points.brief: Split a composite shape into simple shapes, then add their areas, or subtract a cut-out part, and trace the outside edge for the perimeter.

points.title: Circumference of a circle
points.brief: The circumference is π times the diameter, C = πd, or 2πr using the radius.

points.title: Area of a circle
points.brief: A circle's area is π times the radius squared, A = πr², so a circle of radius 5 cm has area about 78.5 cm².

points.title: Volume and capacity of prisms
points.brief: A prism's volume is cross-section area times length, and capacity links to volume, since 1 cm³ holds 1 mL and 1000 cm³ holds 1 L.

points.title: Duration and 24-hour time
points.brief: Converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time, such as 3:45 pm as 1545, and working out how long an event lasts.

points.title: Time zones
points.brief: Places in different time zones keep different clock times, so adding or subtracting the time difference gives the local time somewhere else.

points.title: Rates and best buys
points.brief: A rate compares two quantities with different units, such as km/h or $/kg, and unit rates show which of two deals is the better buy.

points.title: Pythagoras' theorem for the hypotenuse
points.brief: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, c² = a² + b².

points.title: Pythagoras' theorem for a shorter side
points.brief: To find a shorter side, subtract the square of the known short side from the square of the hypotenuse, a² = c² − b², then take the square root.

points.title: Tests for congruent triangles
points.brief: Two triangles are congruent if they match by SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS, so they are the same shape and size.

points.title: Similar shapes and scale factor
points.brief: Similar shapes have equal angles and sides in the same ratio, and the scale factor is a side of the image divided by the matching side of the original.

points.title: Properties of quadrilaterals
points.brief: Congruent triangles explain the properties of quadrilaterals, such as a parallelogram's opposite sides being equal and its diagonals bisecting each other.

points.title: Locating points in three dimensions
points.brief: A point in space is given by three coordinates, (x, y, z), measured along three axes at right angles to each other.

points.title: Census, sample, experiment and observation
points.brief: A census collects data from a whole population, a sample from part of it, and experiments and observations are other ways to collect data, each with costs and limits.

points.title: Primary and secondary data
points.brief: Primary data is collected yourself for your question, and secondary data comes from someone else, such as a government report.

points.title: Random and non-random sampling
points.brief: In a random sample every member has an equal chance of being picked, while non-random samples, such as asking only friends, can give biased results.

points.title: Sample size and variation
points.brief: Different random samples from the same population give different results, and larger samples vary less and estimate the population better.

points.title: Making inferences from a sample
points.brief: A sample's results are used to estimate something about the whole population, such as its mean, while accepting that the estimate is uncertain.

points.title: Complementary events
points.brief: An event and its complement, not the event, have probabilities that add to 1, so if P(rain) = 0.3 then P(no rain) = 0.7.

points.title: Two-way tables
points.brief: A two-way table shows every combination of two events, such as rolling a die and tossing a coin, and is used to find probabilities.

points.title: Venn diagrams
points.brief: Overlapping circles show events, where the overlap is A and B, and everything inside either circle is A or B.

points.title: Tree diagrams for two events
points.brief: Each branch of a tree diagram shows an outcome, and following the branches lists every combined outcome of two steps.
